TOKYO, Oct 13 : Japanese manufacturer Omron will buy US industrial PC firm Onlogic and its parent company, Interlogic, for $675 million, the company said on Tuesday. The acquisition is intended to develop Omron's physical artificial intelligence services within its industrial automation business, the company said in a news release. • Onlogic is a developer, manufacturer and seller of industrial PCs, with which Omron hopes to combine its high-precision control technology to develop physical AI platforms and expand its customer base in the US. • Onlogic's parent, Interlogic, will become a wholly owned subsidiary of Omron. Onlogic will continue to operate as an independent business, retaining its brand and current management team, the release said.

Oct 12 : Oil prices edged lower on Tuesday after climbing by nearly $2 a barrel in the previous session, as traders assessed supply risks from attacks on Saudi Arabia while weighing the prospect of additional diesel supplies from Russia. Brent crude futures fell 61 cents, or 0.57 per cent, to $106.04 a barrel by 0000 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down 47 cents, or 0.5 per cent, at $93.27 a barrel. Brent futures settled at $106.65 a barrel on Monday, the highest since September 15. US President Donald Trump said Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine.

Additional supplies could help alleviate tightness in global fuel markets, tempering some of the supply concerns that have supported crude prices recently. However, lawmakers from both parties in the US complained Trump's agreement with Putin appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine. "Fresh diesel supply from Russia and steadier Saudi flows are offering some relief, yet the market still looks more worried about the risk of further hits to ships or pipelines in the Gulf than it is reassured by extra barrels," Tim Waterer, KCM Trade chief analyst, said. "Until we see clearer signs of de-escalation, the path of least resistance still leans higher," he said. Concerns over the vulnerability of Gulf energy infrastructure and shipping lanes remained in focus after Iran-aligned Houthis struck Riyadh's international airport over the weekend, while tanker attacks were reported near the Strait of Hormuz. The incidents threatened to derail a recovery in Middle East supplies seen in September, and have reinforced fears of further disruptions along one of the world's most important energy transit routes. Ministers of OPEC and non-OPEC Participating Countries in the Declaration of Cooperation said shipping and insurance costs have surged to unprecedented levels of over one-third of the commodity value, impeding efficient movement of crude oil and products. OPEC has revised down its oil demand growth forecast for this year to 400,000 barrels per day from 1.4 million bpd at the start of the year, in line with developments throughout the year, Haitham Al Ghais, Secretary General of the organisation said on Monday.

Source: Reuters

FAST

TOKYO, Oct 13 : Japan's wholesale prices rose 6.8 per cent in the year to September, according to data released on Tuesday, slowing from the previous month but highlighting mounting inflationary pressure that keeps alive market expectations of a near-term interest rate hike. The data will be among the factors that the Bank of Japan will scrutinise when its board produces fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts at this month's policy meeting. The rise in the corporate goods price index, which measures the price companies charge each other for their goods and services, compared with the median market forecast for a 7.6 per cent increase. It slowed from a 7.6 per cent gain in August. The yen-based import price index surged 24.5 per cent in September from a year earlier, the data released by the BOJ showed, a sign that the currency's weakness continued to push up the cost of raw material imports.

"Wholesale inflation will likely re-accelerate given strong uncertainty over the Middle East conflict, which is keeping crude oil prices elevated," said Masato Koike, a senior economist at Sompo Institute Plus. "But there's no sign of inflationary pressure accelerating sharply for the time being," heightening the chance that the BOJ will stand pat in October and wait until December to raise interest rates again, he said. A recent spike in wholesale inflation was among the factors that the BOJ cited as evidence of mounting price pressures behind its decision to raise interest rates in June and September. While the prices of farm products fell 13.3 per cent in September from a year earlier due largely to plunging prices for rice, a broad range of other goods recorded price rises, including processed food, electric machinery and telecommunications equipment, the data showed. Prices of chemical goods rose 13.3 per cent, plastic products increased 12.8 per cent and non-ferrous metals goods were up 40.2 per cent, a sign of the increasing cost firms were facing from the weak yen, the US-Israeli war on Iran and robust AI-related demand, the data showed. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda has said the key to the pace and timing of future rate hikes would be the extent to which such upward pressure on wholesale prices spreads to consumer inflation, as well as how that could affect consumption. Recent data showed core consumer inflation in Tokyo, which is considered a leading indicator of nationwide price trends, accelerated in September at its fastest pace in 10 months. Sources have told Reuters the BOJ may signal this month that underlying inflation has roughly hit its 2 per cent target, highlighting its readiness to raise rates again in the coming months. The BOJ raised its key rate to a 31-year high last month, while signalling its entry into a phase focused on preventing underlying inflation from overshooting its target, raising the prospect of tighter policy. At the meeting on October 29 and 30, the BOJ will release fresh quarterly growth and inflation forecasts that will be closely watched by market participants for clues to the timing of the next rate hike. Many analysts expect the central bank to raise interest rates again by the end of this year.

Source: Reuters

Oct 12 : The New York Times, Agence France-Presse and The Economist on Monday joined more than 40 publishers in a coalition aimed at preventing AI firms from using or profiting from their content without permission. The Standards for Publisher Usage Rights (SPUR) coalition, launched in February, now has more than 80 members across over 20 countries. New members include The Atlantic and Brazil's National Association of Newspapers, joining founding members such as the Financial Times, BBC and Associated Press. Publishers are stepping up legal efforts to prevent AI companies from using their content without permission to train large language models. Earlier this month, USA Today and several newspapers it owns sued OpenAI, alleging copyright infringement. OpenAI and its backer, Microsoft, also face similar copyright claims from prominent authors and news organizations, including the New York Times.

SPUR, which is funded entirely by its members, is developing industry-wide standards and technical systems to help publishers track and control how AI companies use their content and facilitate licensing agreements, according to its website. "Intellectual property protection and technological advancement can and must co-exist," Rebecca Grossman-Cohen, the New York Times' head of strategic partnerships and chief of staff, said in a statement. Publishers are also grappling with declining referral traffic as search engines roll out AI-generated answers that allow users to consume information without clicking through to websites. Google organic-search referrals to more than 2,500 websites fell 33 per cent globally between November 2024 and November 2025, according to a Reuters Institute report, citing data from Chartbeat. SPUR said it recently introduced its Content Telemetry Standard, designed to standardize how AI agents record and report their use of media content, as part of efforts to ensure creators are compensated for their work.

FAST

HOUSTON, Oct 12 : Dense heavy crude, which oil refiners around the world favor for its typically low cost, is piling up in the Americas as soaring freight rates have stifled exports and US refiners have been running close to their limits. The glut in North and South America has opened an unusual split in the global oil market, as buyers in Asia and Europe struggle with supply shortages and benchmark prices hold above $100 a barrel. Heavy crude is a denser type of oil that Asian, many US, and some European refineries are typically configured to process. It is usually cheaper than light crude, offering refiners better margins, when shipping costs are affordable. “It’s all freight,” said Scott Shelton, an energy specialist at TP ICAP. Venezuela, the US and Canada all produce more oil than they consume, he said, so they rely on exports to Asia to balance their crude markets.

With US diesel prices soaring, the cheap, stranded barrels should be getting snapped up in a diesel-starved market, since heavy crude yields more of the fuel than lighter grades. But Gulf Coast refiners have already bought as much as they can process, analysts and traders said. Venezuelan exports have surged since the US captured former President Nicolas Maduro in January, then started pushing to reactivate the country's oil sector. Canadian output is at a record and Washington has released more than 130 million barrels from its emergency reserve. The cost of hiring a supertanker from the US Gulf Coast to Asia, meanwhile, has more than quintupled since February, as ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman tie up vessels worldwide. "You need a ship and the price of ships are going up, and the availability ships are going down," Shelton said. Flagship Canadian, Colombian and Ecuadorian heavy crude grades have all eased more than $10 a barrel to trade at their lowest level in six weeks, according to price reporting agency Argus Media. Prices for Western Canada Select, excluding shipping or insurance costs, was around $74 on Thursday; Colombia's main grade Vasconia was trading at around $84; and Ecuador's Oriente was trading at around $76, Argus said. Venezuelan crude excluding shipping costs was trading around $74.50 a barrel on Thursday, two traders said. Shipping oil on a supertanker from the US Gulf Coast to Europe was estimated to cost around $46 million, or $24.50 a barrel, last week, including ship-to-ship transfer and other costs, according to Georgios Sakellariou, a Signal Maritime analyst. That compares with $6.5 million or around $4 a barrel before the Iran war broke out in late February. The cost of a tanker from the Americas to Asia rose to more than $80 million, or about $40 a barrel, last week compared with around $10-15 million near the start of the year. US REFINERS MAXED OUT US refineries have operated at about 93.5 per cent capacity on an average weekly basis so far this year, according to the Energy Information Administration. That is the highest level in 28 years as they crank out as much as fuel as they can to profit from record high diesel prices. While those refineries are complex and geared to run a heavier crude slate, they can only process it up to a certain percentage of their total capacity. "While Venezuela and US emergency barrels have been a factor for months now, leading to near maximum US coker utilization, high freight is now a further headwind to shipping these barrels east and is forcing heavy sour storage builds in the Americas," Irwin added. Cokers convert residual crude oil into feedstocks for diesel and gasoline production, and a heavier crude slate requires them to run at a higher capacity. Many US refineries are also configured for offshore Gulf of Mexico crude such as Mars Sour, rather than Canadian or Venezuelan oil that must be mixed with lighter feedstock.

Source: Reuters

Oct 12 : Bumble is in advanced talks to be taken private by Ithaca Holdings in a deal valuing the dating app operator at roughly $1 billion, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters on Monday. Shares of the Austin, Texas-based company closed around 50 per cent higher on Monday at $3.80, marking their biggest-ever percentage gain in a single session. The company had a market value of roughly $389 million at Friday's close. Bumble and Ithaca, a holding company for technology businesses founded by Silicon Valley executives Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment. Reuters exclusively reported earlier this year that Bumble was exploring a sale amid slowing growth in the online dating sector.

Dating apps such as Bumble and its larger rival Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, have come under pressure as younger Gen Z subscribers grow disillusioned with endless swiping, leading to softer user engagement. "Going private looks less like a strategic masterstroke and more like an admission that Bumble's current strategy is failing," said PP Foresight analyst Paolo Pescatore. "A change in ownership will not magically fix these fundamental problems." Founded in 2014 by CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble pioneered the "women-first" approach to online dating. But after its $14 billion blockbuster Nasdaq debut in 2021, the company has struggled with a post-pandemic slowdown in growth. Under Wolfe Herd, who returned to the CEO role in March last year after stepping down in January 2024, Bumble has rolled out AI-powered features and new ways for users to connect as it works to reinvigorate growth. Total paying users for Bumble fell more than 11 per cent to about 3.7 million in 2025, while annual revenue declined nearly 10 per cent to about $966 million. In the second quarter ended June 30, total paying users decreased 16.4 per cent to 3.2 million. "AI is not going to be the silver bullet, nor is another round of cost-cutting... Bumble desperately needs to give consumers a compelling reason to return and, more importantly, pay," Pescatore said.

PARIS, Oct 12 : France's LVMH on Monday reported worse-than-expected third-quarter organic sales growth as weak demand for its fashion and leather goods weighed.  Organic sales, which strip out currency swings, rose 1 per cent year-on-year to €18.28 billion ($20.40 billion), compared with the 1.3 per cent increase expected by analysts in Visible Alpha consensus. PARIS, Oct 12 : Hackers forced the temperature of many French supermarket fridges up to 50 degrees Celsius (122°F) overnight, causing fires and food losses at several hundred stores across the country in a major cyberattack. The Paris prosecutor's office said a "large-scale" attack was "affecting connected refrigerators in several major food retailers across France" and reported damage included "food losses and fires". Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu instructed France's National Cybersecurity Agency ANSSI to investigate, a person in his office said. They said France "was coordinating with its European counterparts, as other countries may also be affected," while also investigating whether any other French firms were at risk.

Les Mousquetaires, which owns retailer Intermarche, said around 150 of its stores had been hit, with fridges heated up to 50 degrees Celsius for six hours. It had thrown all the food away to avoid any sanitary risks, a spokesperson said. And Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher said his supermarket had also been hit by the attack. "Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," he wrote on X. Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets had been hit but that the vast majority of its 6,000 stores had not been affected.  Several other supermarket chains, including Monoprix, E.Leclerc and Auchan, did not respond to requests for comment. DUTCH SECURITY ISSUE Dutch supermarket operator Ahold Delhaize, which operates the Netherlands' largest supermarket chain Albert Heijn and has substantial operations in the United States, said it was also dealing with a "security issue" in its network, and had taken several systems offline to protect them. A smartphone app for the retailer told clients that due to a "cybersecurity incident" it was unable to deliver groceries. Online orders represent around 10 per cent of sales for Albert Heijn. Physical stores remained open and Dutch news agency ANP reported that rivals had seen an influx of delivery orders. It was not clear if there was any link between the French supermarket attack and the problems flagged by Ahold Delhaize.  Ahold is the fourth-largest grocery retailer in the US, where websites for its Stop & Shop, Giant, Hannaford and Food Lion stores all had notices saying "site temporarily down". It was unclear if other operations were affected. The source close to Lecornu said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software supplied by Danish company Danfoss. Danfoss said it was "aware of incidents in France affecting a limited number of refrigeration management systems". The affected units "were running outdated firmware", Danfoss said, adding that it had "long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions".

Source: Reuters

LONDON, Oct 12 : Britain's AI Security Institute has been given access to the latest advanced AI models and is working with the US government and major developers, including Google, to assess their safety, AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said on Monday. Britain, which is not home to any major AI developers, is seeking a leading role in efforts to assess and manage the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems. Scrutiny of AI safety has intensified after developers including Anthropic and OpenAI disclosed instances of rogue or undesired behaviour by AI agents. Some industry figures have warned the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity. Monday's announcement, which did not specify all the models the institute is evaluating, comes after reports last month that the White House has asked OpenAI and Anthropic to withhold new models from British testers pending a US review.

Oct 12 : Global smartphone shipments fell 20 per cent on-year to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012, as soaring memory chip costs and supply shortages pressured manufacturers and pushed up prices, preliminary estimates from Counterpoint Research showed on Monday. Rising prices for memory components as AI infrastructure projects corner supplies have driven up production costs and prompted manufacturers to raise retail prices, cut shipments and prioritize profitability over volumes. "Consumers are holding on to their devices longer than estimated, increasingly considering refurbished devices and prioritizing higher-value devices," said Counterpoint senior analyst Shilpi Jain. Samsung retained its top position with a 23 per cent market share, helped by demand for its Galaxy Z Fold8 series and stable component supplies for its mid-range devices. Shipments fell 3 per cent from a year earlier during the quarter.

Xandr relayed data revealing the sexual orientation of users of Grindr, a dating app for LGBTQIA+ people, to companies in automated ad auctions from July 2018 to April 2020. The regulator said companies that traded in people's data could not pass the blame to others. The data protection authority fined Grindr 65 million crowns over the same breaches in 2021.

"Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection." Tech companies such as Anthropic and OpenAI have started disclosing rogue or undesired behaviour by AI agents as part of a global debate about the fast-advancing technology that has included researchers' warnings of an eventual existential threat to humanity. Some companies have called for AI development to slow down, but that has sparked a debate as to whether executives have ulterior motives such as setting rules that preserve the lead of their firms, pre-empting a broader government backlash, or simply slowing breakneck spending. Microsoft's Smith said the one country that was well-placed to lead the way on regulation of AI was Britain, due to the AI Security Institute which was launched under former prime minister, Rishi Sunak.  Smith said officials in Washington viewed London very differently to how they viewed Brussels, which regulates AI based on the level of risk via its AI Act. Britain's institute receives pre-deployment access under voluntary agreements with the major AI models, allowing it to assess their capabilities and risks.  AI Minister Kanishka Narayan has told Reuters that Britain would consider regulating advanced models if the current system proved insufficient.

NEW YORK, Oct 12 : The dollar held at an 18-month high on Monday, supported by safe-haven demand as attacks escalated in the Middle East over the weekend, keeping investors cautious ahead of key US inflation data later this week. The dollar index, which tracks the US currency against six others, was up 0.37 per cent at 102.58, highest since April 2025. Oil prices were volatile after Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis stepped up strikes on Saudi Arabia, and two tankers were attacked over the weekend.  Brent crude futures rose 2.3 per cent to $107.17 a barrel, nearing a two-week high. The attacks overshadowed Sunday's announcement from US President Donald Trump about an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia that seemed imperiled from the get-go, as Kyiv accused Russia of violating the ceasefire overnight.

Brent crude is still nearly 45 per cent above where it was before the US-Israeli war with Iran started. Meanwhile, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said on Monday that the Federal Reserve should move "relatively quickly" to a restrictive policy to control inflation she sees as more broad based. Investors have been increasing bullish positions on the dollar, which as of the week ended October 7 came to about $36 billion, up from $8.4 billion three weeks ago, largely at the expense of the euro. "We aren’t convinced this latest bout of risk aversion will translate into sustained dollar strength," said Joel Kruger, market strategist at LMAX Group in London, citing cooling economic data, inflation pressures moderating, and much of the Fed's expected rate hikes already priced into the market. "We see limited scope for additional dollar upside."  SPOTLIGHT MOVES TO US INFLATION DATA  Wednesday's US consumer inflation report, one of the last major economic releases before the Fed's policy meeting this month, could be critical in determining the near-term direction of the dollar.  US consumer sentiment deteriorated further in early October, as the rising cost of living because of the Middle East conflict soured households' views of the economy. The Fed raised rates last month for the first time since 2023 to rein in inflation. Traders are pricing in a 78 per cent chance of the Fed standing pat this month, up from 51 per cent a month earlier, the CME FedWatch tool showed. "The real focus is on the CPI number this week - it is likely to be running hot," said Marc Chandler, chief market strategist at Bannockburn Global Forex in New York. He added that a rate hike before an election is so uncommon that "the bar is kind of high" for the Fed to act. Investors have grown worried about the sharp selloffs in bond markets that have driven borrowing costs across the globe to multi-decade highs.  The euro fell 0.4 per cent to $1.1156, near a 17-month low, after clocking a fifth straight week of losses last week, driven by investor angst around France's fiscal health before the 2027 presidential election. The spread between French 10-year yields and safer German yields traded at 140 basis points. Last week it neared 160 bps, the most since 2012. "There's been no improvement and no real clear guidance as to what's going to make things better in the short term," said Dan Tobon, head of G10 FX strategy at Citi in New York. "What's the reason to buy European debt, to buy euro here? It's hard to find one, and so we just kind of keep drifting off." The US dollar rose 0.2 per cent to 158.66 yen, while the pound slipped 0.2 per cent at $1.3203.

Source: Reuters

FAST

NEW DELHI, Oct 12 : Oil prices slipped on Monday on expectations of more Russian supplies after US President Donald Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to halt attacks on each other's energy facilities following a US diesel-supply deal with Moscow. Brent crude futures fell 11 cents, or 0.11 per cent, to $104.61 a barrel by 0627 GMT while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $91.36 a barrel, down 49 cents, or 0.53 per cent. Both benchmarks were down more than 1 per cent earlier in the session. ICE gasoil futures fell 3 per cent to $1,436 per metric ton after President Trump said on Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons (2.25 million barrels) of diesel to US and global markets. Russia would supply another 500,000 tons in November and a further 1 million tons "immediately thereafter", Trump added. The daily diesel consumption globally is forecast at close to 29 million barrels, according to the International Energy Agency.

Trump also unexpectedly announced on Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy ceasefire, but Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he was still waiting to see details of the energy ceasefire while Russia did not comment. The announcements eased some of the immediate supply pressure, Tim Waterer, KCM Trade chief analyst, said. "Questions remain over the validity and longevity of any such ceasefire, and without clearer evidence that it will actually hold, the extent of the pullback is likely to stay limited," he added. IEA's Executive Director Fatih Birol said on Sunday that all members should assess whether additional diesel releases are necessary and that countries which have not yet fully delivered pledged volumes accelerate their remaining releases prioritising diesel. CRUDE SUPPORTED BY MIDDLE EAST CONFLICT However, the Middle East conflict continued to support Brent crude at above $100 a barrel. The Houthis claimed responsibility for a Saturday strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, while Saudi authorities reported that people were injured in a new attack on the airport on Sunday. US President Donald Trump said on Saturday the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. In addition, more attacks on tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz have been reported so far this month, threatening to dampen a recovery in Middle East crude exports seen in September. A tanker was struck by a drone in the vicinity of Sohar anchorage, Oman, while another was damaged by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported over the weekend. Goldman Sachs raised its Brent crude price forecast for December to $90 a barrel, up from $85 previously, its analysts led by Daan Struyven said in a note. "We maintain our base case that continued adaptation of Mideast supply will eventually reduce crude oil prices, while potential renewed escalation still poses significant net upside risk," the analysts said, estimating a risk premium of just over $20 a barrel. "We forecast WTI prices, which are unusually low vs Brent because of high US-Europe shipping costs, to average $81 in December 2026 and $73 in 2027," they added. In the Gulf of Mexico, energy majors Shell, Chevron and BP were seeking to redeploy personnel and restore production at their platforms after Hurricane Isaias made landfall early on Saturday.

Source: Reuters
